 End of daylight saving time leads to more wildlife vehicle collisions
 It’s a scary time to be out on the road. Beware! 
 Wildlife & wild places 
 October 26, 2026 
 X 
 Facebook 
 LinkedIn 
 Email 
 Zahra Rothman | Used by permission 
 The end of daylight savings results in a steep increase in wildlife vehicle collisions 
 Take Action 
 Close 
 Tell your U.S. senators: Support wildlife crossings 
 Tell your U.S. senators: Support wildlife crossings 
 Take Action 
 Andrew Rothman 
 Director, Wildlife Campaigns, Environment America
 Steve Blackledge 
 Senior Director, Conservation America Campaign, Environment America
 This Saturday will be an extra long Halloween. We will turn back our clocks as daylight saving time comes to end. This simple clock shift, designed to manage darkness, creates more danger than one might think.  
 When we fall back to standard time, we change our driving patterns, and our afternoon commutes are suddenly in the dark. And while we change the times of our daily patterns by an hour, animals certainly do not. With animals such as deer and elk in their breeding season or “rut”, and other animals fattening up for winter, the time change becomes a real killer…literally.  
 In the four weeks following the fall time change, there are 6% more car crashes in general. Dig deeper and research shows that there are 28% more nighttime crashes and “collisions with deer increase by 16% in the week following the autumn clock change.”  
 No one wants to hit a deer or any other animal while out on the road, yet according to State Farm Insurance, 1 out of 139 American drivers are involved in animal related collisions each year. Furthermore, it is estimated that there are 1 million animals killed on roads every day. Many of these occur this time of the year. Nearly 10% of all deer vehicle collisions occur in the two weeks following or autumnal time change.  
 EcoFlight | Used by permission 
 Roads that see over 10,000 cars a day create barriers for wildlife, which is why wildlife crossings are needed. 
 Reconnecting nature  
 Our elk, bobcats, bighorn sheep and even turtles need room to roam. Yet, America is more fragmented by roads, fences and development than ever before. Currently there are 4.2 million miles of public roads in the U.S. Just in 2023, we added another 1,749 miles of public roads in the U.S. Between 1980 and 2008 we were adding 6,500 miles of roads per year on average. 
 As we expand our roads system, we continue to infringe upon wildlife and their habitat and force animals to attempt dangerous crossings. More than 1 million large animals (like moose, deer or bear) are killed on America’s roads each year. The fall, and the increase in wildlife vehicle collisions, presents an opportunity for us to examine how our roads impact wildlife.  
 Roadside Wildlife Count 
 This year, between October 2nd and 11th, Environment America Research & Policy Center, along with our state partner organizations, held the 2026 Roadside Wildlife Count. This event asked everyday people to help contribute data on wildlife seen along roads across the country.  
 The results, some 1,400 observations of wildlife along roads; 60% of these observations were of dead animals. While this is just a snap shot data from around 500 individuals across 33 states it’s a window to the carnage that roads create for our wildlife.  
 Emma Lopez-Rivera | TPIN 
 Data from the 2026 Roadside Wildlife Count 
 Finding the light in wildlife crossings 
 While our days are darker this time of year, there is a shining light of hope for reducing wildlife vehicle collisions. Wildlife crossings.  
 Wildlife crossings can take different forms, such as a tunnel or culvert under a road or a bridge over a road. Officials have also modified the undersides of existing bridges to make them more passable to animals. When they are built with fencing to guide animals to the crossing, wildlife crossings can reduce wildlife-vehicle collisions by up to 97% . 
 These structures help reconnect habitat and allow wildlife to safely migrate, find mates, and access the basic resources they need to survive. In some cases, like in Colorado where the new Greenland Overpass opened in December 2025, the structures are allowing species such as pronghorn to cross roads they haven’t been able to cross in decades.  
 While we don’t have a take on the debate about changing our clocks twice a year, we do have a take on wildlife crossings; and that is that we need more investments in wildlife crossings.  
 Specifically, we need the U.S. Congress to reauthorize the Wildlife Crossing Pilot Program and increase funding for the program to at least $100 M a year for five years in the next Surface Highway Transportation bill.  
 This Halloween, when we fall back, join us in telling the Senate to increase funding for wildlife crossings. 
 Authors
 Andrew Rothman 
 Director, Wildlife Campaigns, Environment America
 As the Wildlife Campaigns Director for Environment America, Andrew’s primary focus is to make sure that our country invests in and builds wildlife crossings and wildlife corridors. By building bridges and underpasses, and by conserving land along the migration routes, we can make sure that animals have room to roam. In addition, Andrew works to better fund state wildlife agencies, and to ensure the Endangered Species Act stays strong. Andrew lives in Denver with his wife and daughter. In his free time you may find Andrew attending sporting events, birding or on the trail exploring the Rocky Mountains.
 Steve Blackledge 
 Senior Director, Conservation America Campaign, Environment America
 Steve directs Environment America’s efforts to protect our public lands and waters and the species that depend on them. He led our successful campaign to win full and permanent funding for our nation’s best conservation and recreation program, the Land and Water Conservation Fund. He previously oversaw U.S. PIRG’s public health campaigns. Steve lives in Sacramento, California, with his family, where he enjoys biking and exploring Northern California.
